teile.einleitung: The forest dung beetle is a beetle with a shiny blue-black body that crawls about mainly on paths in the forest. It eats the droppings of animals and buries them as food for its larvae. In this way it is an important helper that keeps the forest floor clean and fertile.
wichtigste: The forest dung beetle lives mainly in forests, especially beech woods.
Its scientific name is Anoplotrupes stercorosus.
It grows to about 12 to 19 millimetres long.
Its underside shines metallic blue, violet or green.
It feeds mainly on droppings, and sometimes on fungi.
It digs tunnels in the ground and stores droppings there for its larvae.
It develops in complete metamorphosis: egg, larva, pupa, beetle.

abschnitte.text: The forest dung beetle is 12 to 19 millimetres long and has a domed, shiny blue-black body. The underside shimmers **metallic** blue, violet or green. On the wing cases you can see seven fine lengthwise grooves. It looks very similar to the common dung beetle, but stays smaller.

The forest dung beetle is found all over Europe, in the east as far as western Siberia. It lives from the lowlands up to about 2000 metres and is also common in Switzerland. You find it especially often in **beech woods**. In summer and autumn you often see the beetles crawling singly across forest paths.

The beetle eats mainly the **droppings** of animals such as roe deer, red deer, wild boar or foxes. Sometimes it also eats fungi or tree sap. It belongs to the dung beetle family, but does not roll balls like the scarab beetles. Instead it pulls the dung down into the ground.

In spring, males and females dig a vertical **tunnel** into the ground together. Side tunnels branch off from this passage and end in small chambers. The female works underground, and the male carries the dug-out earth outside. Into each chamber goes an egg together with a store of droppings.

A **larva** hatches from the egg and eats the store of droppings in its chamber. The larva grows for about a year and spends the winter in the ground. In spring it turns into a pupa, and in summer the finished beetle hatches. But it can only breed itself the following spring.

Forest dung beetles are important **recyclers** in the forest. By burying droppings, they bring nutrients into the soil, and the forest floor is loosened. In this way animal droppings and the fly larvae living in them also disappear faster. On the underside of the beetle you often see small mites that let it carry them to the next dung heap.

begriffe.erklaerung: A beetle family whose members feed on animal droppings.
Everything that parent animals do so that their young grow up well.
Making chirping sounds by rubbing two parts of the body together.
The hard front wings of a beetle, which protect the delicate hind wings.

gewusst: Forest dung beetles can make chirping sounds by rubbing parts of the body together.
If a forest dung beetle lies on its back, it often has trouble getting back on its feet.

teile.einleitung: Turritopsis dohrnii is a tiny jellyfish that has become famous as the “immortal jellyfish”. It can change back into a younger stage and so, in a way, begin its life afresh. This makes it especially long-lived and fascinates researchers all over the world.
wichtigste: Turritopsis dohrnii is called the immortal jellyfish.
The fully grown jellyfish is only about 4 to 5 millimetres in size.
Under stress, injury or in old age, it can turn back into a polyp.
New, young jellyfish arise again from this polyp.
Originally the species comes from the Mediterranean.
It is not completely immortal, because it can be eaten or die of disease.
Researchers hope to learn more about ageing from it.

abschnitte.titel: What kind of animal is it?
abschnitte.text: Turritopsis dohrnii belongs to the **cnidarians**, like all jellyfish, corals and sea anemones. More exactly, it counts as a hydrozoan. The adult jellyfish is transparent, bell-shaped and smaller than a fingernail. It is named after the German zoologist Anton Dohrn, who founded a famous marine research station in Naples.

Normally a **polyp** that stays fixed in place grows from a larva and buds off small jellyfish. These grow up, reproduce and in most species die afterwards. Turritopsis dohrnii, however, can reverse this path. If it is injured, starves or grows old, it sinks to the bottom and turns back into a polyp.

In the change back, its **cells** change their job, and cells of the jellyfish become cells of the polyp. This process is called **transdifferentiation**. Later many genetically identical jellyfish can arise from the new polyp. This ability was discovered in the 1990s by researchers in Italy.

Originally the species lives in the **Mediterranean**, for example off the Italian coast. By now very similar Turritopsis jellyfish are found in many seas of the world. They probably travelled along in the ballast water of ships. Because they are so small, swimmers hardly notice them.

The jellyfish is an exciting model for **research into ageing**. Scientists study its genes in order to understand how cells stay young or renew themselves. One day this could help in medicine, for example in the healing of tissue. For people, however, there is no way of making themselves young again like this jellyfish.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of animals with stinging cells that includes jellyfish, corals and sea anemones.
The form of a cnidarian that stays fixed in place and looks like a small tube.
A cell changes its job and becomes a different kind of cell.
The sequence of life stages of a living thing.

gewusst: In theory a Turritopsis jellyfish could repeat its life cycle as often as it likes.
In the laboratory, a jellyfish has been seen to change back several times in a row.
The immortal jellyfish is about as big as a lentil.

teile.einleitung: Ursus is the scientific name of a genus of bears. It includes, for example, the brown bear, the polar bear and the American black bear. The word Ursus is Latin and simply means bear.
wichtigste: Ursus is a genus of the bear family (Ursidae).
The brown bear and the polar bear both belong to the genus Ursus.
Other species are the American black bear and the Asiatic black bear.
Ursus is the Latin word for bear.
The polar bear and the Kodiak bear, a subspecies of the brown bear, are the largest land predators.
Brown bears and polar bears are so closely related that they can have young together.
In Switzerland, single brown bears from Italy occasionally roam about.

abschnitte.text: In biology every species gets a two-part **scientific name**. The first part names the **genus**, the second the species. The brown bear is called Ursus arctos, and the polar bear Ursus maritimus. This shows that both belong to the same genus. Ursus is Latin and means bear, and arctos is the Greek word for bear.

The genus Ursus is usually counted as having four species: the **brown bear**, the **polar bear**, the American black bear and the Asian black bear, also called the moon bear. Some researchers also count the sloth bear and the sun bear. The giant panda and the spectacled bear are bears too, but belong to other genera. The cave bear, which lived in the Ice Age also in Switzerland, is extinct.

The polar bear and the brown bear are closely related, and the polar bear developed a few hundred thousand years ago from ancestors like brown bears. That is why they can even have young together, and the crosses are sometimes called **cappuccino bears** or pizzlies. The polar bear lives in the Arctic and hunts seals on the sea ice. The brown bear lives in forests and mountains in Europe, Asia and North America and eats plants, berries, insects and meat.

Bears of the genus Ursus are big and strong, with a massive body, short tails and strong claws. They walk as **plantigrades**, that is, with the whole sole of the foot on the ground, as we humans do. Most are **omnivores**. Many spend the winter in a den in a winter rest, in which the body temperature drops only slightly.

The last brown bear in Switzerland was shot in 1904 in the Lower Engadine. Since 2005, single young bears have repeatedly wandered from Trentino in Italy into the Engadine and the Münstertal. The bear is the heraldic animal of Bern and Appenzell. In the **Bear Park** in Bern you can watch brown bears.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of very closely related species, for example Ursus.
An animal that walks on the whole sole of the foot.
An animal that eats both plants and meat.
A long sleep in winter in which the body cools down only a little.

gewusst: The constellation Great Bear is called Ursa Major in Latin.
The name Arctic comes from the Greek word arktos for bear, because the constellation stands in the north.
A polar bear has black skin under its white fur.

teile.einleitung: Whales are huge mammals that spend their whole lives in the water. Although they look like fish, they breathe with lungs like us and have to come up to the surface to take in air. Whales include the blue whale, the largest animal that has ever lived on Earth.
wichtigste: Whales live in the sea, but breathe with lungs like us humans.
They are mammals, give birth to live young and nurse them with milk.
A distinction is made between baleen whales and toothed whales.
Dolphins and porpoises are also whales.
The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived.
Whales breathe through a blowhole on the head.
Their ancestors lived on land about 50 million years ago.

abschnitte.text: Whales form a group of sea mammals with about 90 species. They are not fish, but **mammals** like cows or humans. Their tail fin, the **fluke**, lies horizontally and moves up and down, while fish move their tail fin from side to side. Under the skin, a thick layer of fat, the blubber, protects against the cold.

Whales breathe through a **blowhole** on top of the head, which is a kind of nostril. When breathing out, they blow out a fountain of air and water droplets, the blow. Large whales can dive for a long time: the sperm whale stays under water for over an hour and dives over 2000 metres deep. So that they do not drown in their sleep, in many whales only one half of the brain rests at a time.

**Baleen whales** such as the blue whale, humpback whale and fin whale have no teeth, but plates of baleen made of horn in the mouth. With them they sieve huge amounts of small crustaceans such as krill out of the water. The blue whale grows to about 30 metres long and can weigh well over 100 tonnes. Humpback whales are famous for their long songs.

The **toothed whales** include the sperm whale, orca, dolphins and porpoises. They hunt fish and squid, and the orca even catches seals. Toothed whales find their prey by **echolocation**: they send out clicking sounds and listen for the echo. The sperm whale is the largest toothed whale and the animal with the heaviest brain.

Whales usually give birth to a single young one alive, often tail first. The mother nurses it with very fatty milk. Many whales live in groups called **pods**. Orcas and sperm whales live in close family groups that are led by older females.

The ancestors of whales lived on land about 50 million years ago and had four legs. Over millions of years they adapted to life in the water. Their closest living relatives on land today are the **hippopotamuses**. No whales live in Switzerland, but fossil remains of sea animals show that the Central Plateau was once covered by a sea.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal whose young are fed on their mother's milk.
Horny plates in the mouth of baleen whales that work like a sieve.
The breathing opening on top of a whale's head.
Finding the way by sound, whose echo reveals the position of things.

gewusst: Blue whales are among the loudest animals in the world, and their deep calls carry hundreds of kilometres.
The song of humpback whales can be heard under water for many kilometres.
A newborn blue whale drinks hundreds of litres of milk every day.

teile.einleitung: Birds are vertebrates with feathers, wings and a beak that lay eggs. Most of them can fly, but some such as the ostrich or the penguin stay on the ground or in the water. There are about 11 000 species of bird on Earth, from the tiny hummingbird to the giant ostrich.
wichtigste: Birds are the only living animals with feathers.
All birds lay eggs with a hard shell of lime, and a well-known example is the hen.
Instead of teeth, birds have a beak made of horn.
Many bird bones are hollow and therefore light.
Birds are warm-blooded, and their body temperature is usually around 40 degrees.
Birds are descended from dinosaurs.
About 200 species of bird nest in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The most important feature of birds is their **feathers**. Feathers keep them warm, make flying possible and, with their colours, serve as camouflage or for display. The front legs have turned into **wings**. Birds have a beak without teeth and lay eggs, which they usually sit on in a nest. Their heart beats fast, and they have a high body temperature.

To fly, birds need a light body and strong **chest muscles**. Many bones are hollow and run through with air chambers. The wings are curved, so that lift is created in flight. Their special breathing system with **air sacs** supplies them well with oxygen even at great heights. Some birds such as swifts stay in the air without a break for months.

Birds developed more than 150 million years ago from small, feathered **dinosaurs**. A famous fossil is Archaeopteryx from southern Germany, a mixed creature with feathers, teeth and a long tail. That is why researchers say today that birds are living dinosaurs. The crocodiles are their closest living relatives among the other reptiles.

There are about 11 000 **species of bird** worldwide. The smallest is the bee hummingbird, a hummingbird from Cuba weighing about 2 grams. The largest is the African ostrich, which can grow over 2.5 metres tall. Penguins cannot fly, but are excellent swimmers. Many species are **migratory birds** that fly south in autumn.

About 200 species of bird nest in Switzerland, including the blackbird, great tit, golden eagle and bearded vulture. The **Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach** studies and protects the native birds. Many migratory birds such as swallows and storks spend the winter in Africa. About 40 per cent of the breeding bird species are on the Red List, mainly species of farmland.

The **domestic chicken** is the most common farm animal in the world and supplies eggs and meat. People also keep ducks, geese, turkeys and budgerigars. Birds pollinate flowers, spread seeds and eat insects. Birdwatching is a popular hobby that you can start in your own garden.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal with a backbone, for example a fish, bird or human.
The body keeps its temperature itself, however warm it is outside.
A bird that flies to another area at certain times of year.
A male's wooing of a female, for example with song or dance.

gewusst: There are many more chickens in the world than people.
A swift can fly for up to ten months at a stretch without landing.
The ostrich lays the largest egg of all living birds.

teile.einleitung: The whale shark is the largest fish in the world and can grow as long as a city bus. Despite its size, it is a peaceful giant that filters only tiny living things such as plankton out of the water. It lives in warm seas around the globe and is badly endangered today.
wichtigste: The whale shark is the largest living fish in the world.
The longest reliably documented body length is about 18.8 metres.
It filters tiny living things such as plankton out of the water.
It belongs to the cartilaginous fish and to the order of carpet sharks.
Its family Rhincodontidae contains only a single genus.
Andrew Smith first described it scientifically in 1828.
Every whale shark has its own pattern of light spots.

abschnitte.text: The whale shark is a **shark** and so a fish, not a mammal. It belongs to the class of **cartilaginous fish**, whose skeleton is made of cartilage instead of bone. It gets its name from its size and because it filters its food out of the water in a similar way to baleen whales. In classification it counts in the order of carpet sharks and in the family Rhincodontidae, which contains only a single genus.

The whale shark has a broad, flat head with a huge mouth right at the front. Its dark grey to bluish back is covered with light spots and stripes that form a **pattern** of its own in every animal. Most adult whale sharks grow to about 10 to 12 metres long. The greatest reliably documented length is about 18.8 metres.

The whale shark eats mainly **plankton**, that is, tiny crustaceans, fish eggs, jellyfish and small fish. It swims with its mouth open or sucks in large amounts of water. Sieve-like **gill rakers** hold the food back, and the water flows out again through the gill slits. Although it has thousands of tiny teeth, it hardly needs them for eating.

Whale sharks live in all the tropical and warm seas of the world. They often migrate long distances and sometimes dive very deep. At certain times of year they meet at places with a lot of food, for example at **Ningaloo Reef** in Western Australia, off Mexico or the Philippines. There divers swim with the harmless giants.

The whale shark was first described scientifically in 1828 by the doctor and zoologist **Andrew Smith**. It was based on an animal that had been harpooned in Table Bay near Cape Town in South Africa. The genus name Rhincodon probably means “rasp tooth”. The full scientific name is Rhincodon typus.

Whale sharks give birth to live young that first develop from eggs inside the mother. A female caught in 1995 carried around 300 **embryos** inside her. Because whale sharks grow slowly and become adult late, their populations recover only slowly. Through fishing, bycatch and collisions with ships, the whale shark is regarded today as **endangered**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fish such as sharks and rays whose skeleton is made of flexible cartilage.
Tiny living things that float in the water and drift with the current.
An animal that sieves its food out of the water.
A sieve at the gills that holds back food.

gewusst: You can recognise every whale shark by its pattern of spots, rather as people are recognised by their fingerprints.
A whale shark usually swims along comfortably at only about five kilometres an hour, so about walking pace.

teile.einleitung: Whaling means hunting whales in order to use their fat, their meat and other parts. Over centuries so many whales were killed that some species such as the blue whale almost died out. Today commercial whaling is greatly restricted by an international ban.
wichtigste: People have hunted whales for thousands of years.
In the past many blue whales were hunted for their fat and meat.
From whale fat people obtained train oil, which was used as lamp oil and for soap and margarine.
In the 20th century, factory ships killed more whales than ever before.
The International Whaling Commission was founded in 1946.
Since 1986 an international ban on commercial whaling has been in force.
Some countries such as Japan, Norway and Iceland still go on hunting whales.

abschnitte.text: Even in the Stone Age people hunted whales on the coasts, as old rock pictures show. Peoples of the Arctic such as the **Inuit** used almost everything from a whale: meat and fat to eat, bones for tools and hides for boats. In the Middle Ages the **Basques** in northern Spain became well-known whalers. Later whalers from the Netherlands, England and America sailed on all the seas.

The most important product was **train oil**, an oil from the fat of whales. Lamps burned with it in streets and houses, and it was made into soap and lubricant. The baleen of baleen whales, the **whalebone**, was flexible and was used for corsets and umbrellas. The meat was also eaten.

Around 1870 the Norwegian Svend Foyn developed a **harpoon gun** with an exploding tip. Together with fast steamships, it was now possible to hunt large, fast whales such as the blue whale as well. In the 20th century, huge **factory ships** processed the whales right on the open sea. In the 20th century alone, well over 300 000 blue whales were killed.

Through the hunting, the populations of many whale species collapsed dramatically. Of the blue whale only a tiny fraction was left, and it was close to extinction. In 1946 several states founded the **International Whaling Commission**, IWC for short. Since 1966 the blue whale has been protected worldwide.

In 1982 the IWC decided on a **moratorium**, that is, a pause on commercial whaling, which applied from 1986. Today blue whales and other whales are protected worldwide by this international ban on whaling. Only a small hunt is still allowed for some indigenous peoples who have always lived on whales. Switzerland is also a member of the IWC and works for the protection of whales.

Norway and Iceland go on hunting whales despite the ban, mainly minke whales and fin whales. Japan left the IWC in 2019 and has since hunted commercially again in its own waters. Many whale species are recovering slowly, but dangers such as ship collisions, fishing nets and noise in the sea remain. In many countries today, **whale watching** brings in more money than hunting did in the past.

begriffe.erklaerung: Oil obtained from the fat of whales or fish.
A throwing spear or missile with barbs for catching large sea animals.
An agreed stop or pause on something.
Trips by boat to watch whales in the wild.

gewusst: Before there was paraffin and electricity, many street lamps in Europe burned whale oil.
One blue whale supplied as much oil as several dozen smaller whales put together.

teile.einleitung: The tawny owl is a medium-sized owl with a round head and big dark eyes. It is the most common owl in Switzerland and lives in woods, parks and even in villages and towns. Its call “hooo, hu hu-hooo” can be heard on many nights, but the well-camouflaged bird itself is seldom seen.
wichtigste: The tawny owl is active mainly at night and at dusk.
It lives in woods, parks and also in settlements.
A fully grown tawny owl usually weighs between 400 and 700 grams, and females are heavier than males.
There is a grey and a reddish brown plumage variety.
Its very big eyes see excellently in twilight.
Tawny owl pairs usually stay together for life.
The eggs are incubated for about 28 to 30 days.

abschnitte.text: The tawny owl grows to about 40 centimetres tall and has a round head without **ear tufts**. Its plumage is either grey or reddish brown and patterned with dark streaks, so it is perfectly camouflaged against tree bark. The females are usually heavier than the males. A fully grown bird usually weighs between 400 and 700 grams.

The tawny owl lives in deciduous and mixed woods, in parks, cemeteries and gardens with old trees. It is found in almost all of Europe and is also widespread in Switzerland. Especially important are old deciduous trees with natural **tree holes**, in which it nests and hides by day. But it also accepts nest boxes, barns or church towers.

The tawny owl hunts at night and at dusk from a perch. Its eyes are very big and can see excellently in twilight, and its hearing is so fine that it can hear a mouse under the leaves. Thanks to soft feathers with serrated edges, it flies almost **silently**. It eats mainly mice, but also small birds, frogs, beetles and earthworms, and it coughs up indigestible remains as **pellets**.

The male calls a long drawn-out “hooo, hu hu-hooo”, and the female often answers with a sharp “ku-wit”. Many people recognise only this call, without ever spotting the well-camouflaged bird. A tawny owl pair defends a **territory**, which usually covers a few hectares of forest or built-up area. The pairs often stay together there all their lives.

Tawny owls nest very early in the year, often in February or March. The female usually lays two to four white eggs and sits on them for about 28 to 30 days, while the male brings food. The young leave the hole before they can really fly and then sit on twigs as **branchers**. Such young birds are not abandoned, because the parents go on feeding them.

A wild tawny owl usually lives to be about 5 to 10 years old, and some much older. Dangers are road traffic and the lack of old trees with holes. In Switzerland the tawny owl is not regarded as threatened. Anyone who puts up nest boxes and leaves old trees standing helps it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird of prey of the night with big eyes that point forwards.
A lump of hair and bones that an owl coughs up.
A young bird that has left the nest but cannot really fly yet.
An area that an animal defends against others of its species.

gewusst: A tawny owl can turn its head very far, about three quarters of a full turn.
The well-known owl hoot “hoo-hoo” in films mostly comes from the tawny owl.
Tawny owls defend their nest very bravely and even attack people who come too close.

teile.einleitung: The tundra is a treeless cold steppe in the far north of the Earth, where there are long, icy winters and only short summers. Mainly mosses, lichens, grasses and low shrubs grow here. Typical inhabitants are reindeer, Arctic foxes and ptarmigan.
wichtigste: The tundra is a treeless cold steppe in cold regions.
It lies mainly in the north of Canada, Alaska, Scandinavia and Siberia.
Deep down the ground is frozen all year round, which is called permafrost.
Trees cannot grow here because of the cold and the short summer.
Reindeer travel in large herds through the tundra and eat lichens.
In summer many plants bloom and countless mosquitoes swarm out.
Because of global warming, the permafrost is thawing in many places.

abschnitte.text: The **Arctic tundra** lies north of the great coniferous forests, for example in Alaska, northern Canada, Greenland, northern Scandinavia and Siberia. High in the mountains there are also landscapes like the tundra, which are called **alpine tundra**. In the Alps this is the zone above the tree line. The word tundra comes from Finnish or Sámi and means roughly treeless hill.

In winter it often gets to minus 30 degrees in the tundra, and for months it is almost always dark. The summer lasts only about two months, but then the sun sometimes shines round the clock. Below the surface lies the **permafrost**, a soil that stays frozen permanently. In summer only the top layer thaws, which is why many pools and bogs form.

In the tundra grow **lichens**, mosses, grasses, sedges and dwarf shrubs such as the dwarf birch. The plants stay small and grow close to the ground, where it is warmer and less windy. Many bloom very quickly and brightly in the short summer. Reindeer lichen is one of the most important sources of food for animals.

The best-known animal is the **reindeer**, called caribou in North America, which migrates in huge herds. Other inhabitants are Arctic foxes, lemmings, snowy owls, musk oxen and ptarmigan. Many have a thick coat or plumage and turn white in winter. In summer millions of migratory birds come to breed, because there are then many insects.

In the tundra live peoples such as the **Sámi** in Scandinavia, the Inuit in Canada and Greenland and the Nenets in Siberia. Some of them traditionally keep reindeer. The Arctic is warming faster than the rest of the Earth. When the permafrost thaws, greenhouse gases escape, and houses and roads can sink.

begriffe.erklaerung: Ground that has been frozen without a break for at least two years.
A partnership of a fungus and an alga that also grows in barren places.
The line above or north of which no trees grow any more.
Open land without trees in a very cold climate.

gewusst: Dwarf willows in the tundra are often only a few centimetres tall, although they are many years old.
Well-preserved mammoths have already been found in the permafrost of Siberia.
Reindeer are the only deer in which the females also carry antlers.

teile.einleitung: Toucans are tropical birds from Central and South America that you can recognise at once by their huge, colourful bill. They form the family Ramphastidae and belong to the order of woodpecker-like birds. Their bill is amazingly light and even helps them to control their body temperature.
wichtigste: Toucans form the bird family Ramphastidae in the order of woodpecker-like birds (Piciformes).
The family includes about 40 species in mostly five genera.
The closest relatives of the toucans are the toucan barbets of the genus Semnornis.
The toco toucan (Ramphastos toco) is the largest species, about 55 to 63 centimetres long and 0.5 to 0.9 kilograms in weight.
Its bill is on average about 20 centimetres long in the male.
Inside, the bill is made of airy bone foam under a thin keratin sheath and is therefore light.
In 2009, researchers showed in the journal Science that the bill works as a heat exchanger.

abschnitte.text: Toucans have a **huge bill**, which in some species makes up almost a third of the body length. It is often coloured bright yellow, orange, red, green or black. The plumage is mostly black or green with colourful patches on the throat and rump. Like woodpeckers, toucans have two toes pointing forwards and two backwards, which they use to cling well to branches. The largest species, the **toco toucan**, grows to about 55 to 63 centimetres long.

Although the bill is so big, it is very light. Inside it is made of an airy **bone foam** with many small hollow spaces. On the outside lies a thin sheath of **keratin**, the same substance as our fingernails. This horny layer is built up from overlapping little plates, like roof tiles. Engineers study this structure in order to develop light and stable materials.

abschnitte.titel: The bill as an air conditioner
abschnitte.text: In 2009 researchers showed in the journal **Science** that the bill of the toco toucan works as a **heat exchanger**. When it gets hot, more blood flows through the blood vessels in the bill, and heat is given off. When it gets cool, the blood flow is reduced. In this way the bird can regulate its body temperature cleverly, rather like an elephant with its ears.

Toucans live in forests from Mexico to northern Argentina, many in **tropical rainforest**. The toco toucan is also found in more open landscapes, for example in the Pantanal in Brazil. Toucans eat mainly fruit, but also insects, lizards and the eggs and young of other birds. With the long bill they reach fruit on thin twigs that would not bear their weight. Because they pass out seeds, they help to spread the forest.

Toucans often live in pairs or in small groups and call loudly and harshly. They nest in **tree holes**, for example in old woodpecker holes. The female usually lays 2 to 4 white eggs, and both parents sit on them and feed the young. To sleep, toucans tuck their bill and tail under their plumage and become a small ball of feathers.

Toucans belong to the order of **woodpecker-like birds**, which also includes our woodpeckers. Their closest relatives are the **toucan barbets** of the genus Semnornis. The family includes about 40 species, in five genera under the classification most used today, among them the large toucans (Ramphastos) and the aracaris. Some species are threatened by the felling of rainforests and by the illegal animal trade. In Switzerland you can see toucans only in zoos.

begriffe.erklaerung: A horny substance that hair, nails and feathers are also made of.
Something that passes heat from one place to another.
A bird order that includes woodpeckers, barbets and toucans.
A group of very closely related species.

gewusst: The bill of the toco toucan is almost as long as the rest of its body without the tail.
Toucans sometimes toss fruit into the air with their bill and catch it again.
Young toucans hatch naked and still have a very small bill.

teile.einleitung: Feeding birds means that people offer wild birds extra food, mostly in winter in a bird table or feeder. This gives pleasure, because you can watch tits, finches and robins from close up. For it to really help the birds, however, you should follow a few rules.
wichtigste: Feeding birds takes place mainly in winter, when frost and snow make food scarce.
You should not scatter food straight on the ground, because it quickly gets dirty and wet.
If a lot of food is offered in winter, more great tits survive.
Seed eaters like sunflower seeds, while soft food eaters prefer oat flakes, raisins and apples.
Bread, salted foods and leftovers are unsuitable for birds.
Feeding places have to be kept clean so that diseases do not spread.
A natural garden with berry bushes helps the birds most.

abschnitte.text: In **feeding birds**, people offer wild birds extra food. In Switzerland this happens mainly in **winter**, when the ground is frozen or covered with snow. At the bird table you can watch great tits, blue tits, chaffinches, blackbirds and robins. For many children it is a great introduction to the study of birds.

Birds with strong beaks such as finches and sparrows are **seed eaters** and like sunflower seeds. Blackbirds and robins are **soft food eaters** and prefer oat flakes, raisins, fruit and fat food. Fat balls contain fat with seeds, and you should buy them without a plastic net. Bread, salty food and food scraps harm the birds.

You should not scatter food straight on the ground, because it quickly gets dirty and wet. Germs and mould can form in it. Better are **feeding silos**, where the birds do not walk around in the food. You should clean bird tables regularly with hot water.

The feeding place should stand where **cats** cannot sneak up, for example free-standing on a post. A bush a few metres away offers the birds cover. Panes of glass nearby can be dangerous, because birds fly into them. Stickers or patterns on the window help against this.

Studies show that more great tits survive the winter when a lot of food is offered. However, it is mainly common species that benefit from this, and rare birds hardly do. Experts such as the **Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach** therefore recommend supporting birds above all through a natural garden. Native shrubs such as elder, rowan and hawthorn supply berries and insects all year round.

begriffe.erklaerung: A food dispenser from which only a little food slides down and which stays clean.
A bird that eats mainly seeds and grains.
A bird that prefers insects, berries and soft food.
A ball of fat and seeds that you hang up for birds.

gewusst: A great tit weighs only about 18 grams and in winter has to eat almost a third of its weight every day.
At the bird table there is a pecking order, and bigger birds often drive off smaller ones.
Every year in January, many people count the birds in their garden for research.

teile.einleitung: Tarantulas are large, very hairy spiders that live in warm countries all around the world. They include the goliath birdeater, the heaviest spider in the world. Although many people are afraid of them, they are mostly harmless to us.
wichtigste: Tarantulas form the family Theraphosidae and belong to the large group Mygalomorphae.
According to the World Spider Catalog there are about 1100 to 1200 species.
The goliath birdeater is regarded as the heaviest spider in the world and weighs up to about 175 grams.
Its legs can reach a span of up to about 30 centimetres.
Tarantulas have eight eyes, but still see rather poorly.
They breathe with two pairs of book lungs.
The German name, Vogelspinne or “bird spider”, probably goes back to the naturalist Maria Sibylla Merian.

abschnitte.text: Tarantulas have a strong, densely hairy body and eight long legs. Their **chelicerae**, that is, their biting claws, lie parallel to the long axis of the body and strike from top to bottom. The eight eyes sit close together on a small mound, but the spider relies mainly on fine tactile hairs. For breathing it has two pairs of **book lungs**, and most species have four spinnerets, that is, two pairs.

Tarantulas live in the tropics and subtropics of America, Africa, Asia and Australia. Many species dig burrows in the ground or hide under stones and roots. Others live in trees and build silk tubes there between leaves. The **goliath birdeater** lives in the rainforests in the north of South America.

Tarantulas do not build catching webs, but are **ambush hunters**. They wait at night in front of their hiding place until a prey animal comes past, and then grab it in a flash. Mostly they eat insects such as grasshoppers and cockroaches. Large species sometimes also catch frogs, lizards or mice, but birds only rarely. They paralyse the prey with their venom, and then it is turned liquid with digestive juice.

Many American tarantulas have **urticating hairs** on the abdomen, which they can flick off with their hind legs. These hairs itch badly on the skin and irritate the eyes and nose of attackers. The bite of most species is for people about as painful as a wasp sting. It becomes dangerous at most for people with an allergy.

The male transfers his sperm to the female with the palps on his head. Afterwards he often has to flee quickly so that he is not eaten. The female spins a **cocoon** in which, depending on the species, a few dozen to over a thousand eggs lie. Females of many species can live to over 20 years old, while males mostly live only a few years.

The artist **Maria Sibylla Merian** travelled to Suriname in South America and drew insects and spiders there. In her famous copperplate engraving of 1705, a large spider is eating a hummingbird. For a long time many people doubted the picture, but today we know that such cases occur very rarely. In 1758 Carl Linnaeus described a tarantula as Aranea avicularia, and today it is called Avicularia avicularia.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group of primitive spiders whose biting claws strike downwards.
A breathing organ made of many thin leaves lying on top of each other like the pages of a book.
Fine barbed hairs that the spider flicks at enemies for defence.
The spider sheds its old skin that has become too small, in order to grow.

gewusst: At a moult, a tarantula can even partly regrow lost legs.
The shed skin of a tarantula looks like a second, complete spider.
Tarantulas are among the most popular terrarium animals, in Switzerland too.

teile.einleitung: In complete metamorphosis, an insect develops in four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult animal. The larva looks quite different from the finished insect, like a caterpillar and a butterfly. Experts call this amazing development holometaboly.
wichtigste: Complete metamorphosis has four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult insect.
A dung beetle, for example, develops from the egg through larva and pupa to the beetle.
In the pupa, the body of the larva is completely rebuilt.
Beetles, butterflies, flies, mosquitoes, bees, wasps, ants and fleas go through a complete metamorphosis.
Grasshoppers, dragonflies and bugs, on the other hand, have an incomplete metamorphosis without a pupa.
Larva and adult animal often eat quite different food.
The great majority of all insect species develop with complete metamorphosis.

abschnitte.text: Complete metamorphosis, also called **holometaboly**, is a form of development in insects. A larva hatches from the egg, which eats and grows. After that it changes into a **pupa**, which mostly lies still. From the pupa the adult insect finally hatches, which is called the imago.

The larva is an eating machine and grows fast. Because its skin does not grow with it, it has to moult several times. Larvae have names of their own depending on the animal group: in butterflies they are called **caterpillars**, in flies maggots and in the cockchafer grubs. A cockchafer grub lives three to four years in the soil before it turns into a pupa.

From the outside nothing seems to happen in the pupa, but inside almost the whole body is rebuilt. From small groups of cells, the **imaginal discs**, the wings, legs and eyes of the adult animal arise. This is controlled by hormones. Butterflies form a mummy-like pupa, flies a barrel-shaped pupa and beetles a free pupa, in which you can already see the legs and antennae.

In the garden you can watch the metamorphosis well. The caterpillar of the peacock butterfly eats nettles, turns into a pupa and becomes a colourful butterfly. A maggot in the compost becomes a fly. The **dung beetle** also goes through egg, larva, pupa and beetle, with the larva living in the ground on dung that the parents have buried.

In **incomplete metamorphosis** there is no pupal stage. The young of grasshoppers, bugs or dragonflies already resemble the adults, but do not yet have finished wings. They moult several times and become adult step by step. In complete metamorphosis, on the other hand, the larva and the adult often have no similarity at all.

Because the larva and the adult animal live differently, they do not compete for food. The caterpillar eats leaves, and the butterfly drinks nectar. In this way each stage of life can be specialised for one job: the larva for growing, the adult for breeding and spreading. This strategy is very successful, which is why the majority of all insect species belong to this group.

begriffe.erklaerung: The young stage of an insect that comes after the egg and looks quite different from the adult.
The resting stage in which the larva rebuilds itself into the finished insect.
The finished, adult insect.
The technical word for complete metamorphosis.

gewusst: In some insects the adult animal lives only a few hours or days, while the larva grows for years.
The naturalist Maria Sibylla Merian showed as early as about 1700 that caterpillars and butterflies belong together.

teile.einleitung: Bird migration is the name for the regular journeys that many birds make between their breeding areas and their winter areas. Every autumn millions of birds leave Switzerland and fly south, and in spring they come back. Some cover thousands of kilometres and cross mountains, seas and the Sahara.
wichtigste: Many birds migrate south in autumn because they find too little food here in winter.
Many European migratory birds fly over the Sahara on the way to Africa.
Migratory birds find their way partly by the Earth's magnetic field.
Wild geese often fly in a V formation, because in this way they can save energy.
The lead bird at the front changes regularly in the V formation.
Large flocks of wild geese often rest on big lakes such as Lake Constance.
Many small songbirds migrate at night and rest by day.

abschnitte.text: In winter there are hardly any insects here, and snow covers the ground. Birds such as the barn swallow or the swift then find too little **food**. That is why they fly to warmer regions where there is enough to eat. In spring they come back, because here long days and many insects offer good conditions for raising the young.

**Long-distance migrants** such as the white stork, cuckoo and barn swallow spend the winter in Africa south of the Sahara. Short-distance migrants such as the black redstart fly only as far as the Mediterranean region. **Resident birds** such as the house sparrow or the great tit stay with us all year round. In some species only some animals leave, and they are called partial migrants.

On the way to Africa many birds have to cross the Mediterranean and the **Sahara**. Small songbirds eat their way to a thick layer of fat beforehand, which serves them as fuel. Large soaring birds such as the white stork avoid the open sea and fly over the Strait of Gibraltar or the Bosporus. The Alps are also an obstacle, which is why many birds cross over passes such as the Col de Bretolet.

Migratory birds have a built-in **compass**. They can sense the Earth's magnetic field and steer by the position of the sun. Birds that migrate at night also find their way by the stars. In addition there are landmarks such as coasts, rivers and mountains, which experienced birds recognise.

Large birds such as geese and cranes often fly in a **V formation**. Each bird uses the air swirls of the bird in front of it and so needs less effort. The lead bird at the tip has the hardest time, which is why the animals take turns regularly. In autumn and winter many wild geese rest on big lakes such as Lake Constance.

The Arctic tern flies every year from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back, which is tens of thousands of kilometres. Bar-tailed godwits fly without a break over 11 000 kilometres from Alaska to New Zealand. Researchers attach tiny **geolocators** to birds in order to follow their journeys. In Switzerland the Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach has been studying bird migration since 1924.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird that travels back and forth every year between its breeding area and its winter area.
A bird that stays in the same area all year round.
A place where migratory birds feed and rest on the way.
The restlessness of migratory birds when the time to fly away comes, even in a cage.

gewusst: A young cuckoo finds its way to Africa alone, although it has never met its parents.
The swift stays in the air for months and even sleeps in flight.
In autumn on clear nights, hundreds of thousands of birds cross over Switzerland without our noticing.

teile.einleitung: The loggerhead sea turtle is a large sea turtle with a strikingly broad head. With its especially strong beak it cracks mussels, snails and crabs with ease. It travels through all the warm seas and lays its eggs on sandy beaches, including on the Mediterranean.
wichtigste: The loggerhead is one of the seven species of sea turtle.
Its scientific name is Caretta caretta.
It has a big head and an especially strong beak for cracking mussels.
Its shell is reddish brown and can grow to about a metre long.
It lives in warm and temperate seas all over the world, including the Mediterranean.
The females lay their eggs at night on sandy beaches.
Plastic waste, fishing nets and built-up beaches endanger the species.

abschnitte.text: The loggerhead has a heart-shaped, **reddish brown shell** that usually grows 70 to 100 centimetres long. Adult animals often weigh around 100 kilograms, and some more. Striking is its very **broad head** with strong jaw muscles. Instead of teeth it has a hard horny beak. Its legs have turned into flippers, with which it swims elegantly.

The species lives in tropical and temperate seas, in the Atlantic, the Pacific, the Indian Ocean and in the **Mediterranean**. Young turtles drift for years in the open ocean, often among mats of seaweed. Adults like to stay near the coast. They cover huge distances, and some cross whole oceans.

The loggerhead eats mainly **hard-shelled animals** such as mussels, snails, crabs and sea urchins. With its strong beak it crushes the shells with ease. It also eats jellyfish. Sadly it sometimes mistakes drifting plastic bags for jellyfish and swallows them.

To lay eggs, the females often return to the beach where they themselves hatched. At night they dig a pit in the sand and lay about 100 eggs in it. How warm the sand is decides the **sex** of the young: when it is warm, more females hatch. After about two months the young crawl to the sea at night and find their way by the bright horizon. Well-known **nesting beaches** are in Florida, Greece, Turkey and Cyprus.

Many turtles get caught in **fishing nets** or on long lines and drown. The lights of hotels on beaches lead newly hatched young away from the sea. Plastic waste and the building up of beaches are also big problems. In many countries nesting beaches are therefore guarded and nests marked. Holidaymakers can help by avoiding beaches at night and leaving no rubbish behind.

begriffe.erklaerung: A hard casing of bone that protects the turtle's body.
A hard mouth without teeth, such as turtles and birds have.
A beach where sea turtles bury their eggs.
Animals that end up in fishing nets unintentionally.

gewusst: The loggerhead can stay under water for several hours when it is resting.
Young sea turtles find their way by the Earth's magnetic field, like a compass.
Only a very small share of the young that hatch grow up.

teile.einleitung: The green sandpiper is a slender wading bird that lives by streams, pools and in boggy woods. Unusual for a wader is that it does not nest on the ground, but in old nests of other birds high up in trees. Its chicks therefore have to make a brave leap down right after hatching.
wichtigste: The green sandpiper is a wading bird of the sandpiper and snipe family.
It often nests in old nests of other birds in trees, for example of thrushes.
After hatching, the chicks have to jump from the tree nest to the ground.
It breeds in the boggy woods of northern Europe and Asia.
In Switzerland you see it on migration and sometimes in winter.
It eats water insects, small crustaceans and small fish.
Typical is its constant bobbing of the tail.

abschnitte.text: The green sandpiper is 21 to 24 centimetres long and weighs about 50 to 80 grams. It has a long, dark bill and a dark brown upper side with fine light speckles. In flight the bright **white rump** is striking, which makes a strong contrast with the dark underside of the wings. When standing it bobs its rear end constantly.

The green sandpiper breeds in the northern coniferous forests of Eurasia, from Scandinavia to eastern Siberia. There it lives in **swamp woods**, bogs and on the wooded banks of lakes and streams. In central Europe it breeds, for example, in Poland and in the east of Germany. In Switzerland it does not breed, but it is a regular migrant visitor and occasionally a winter visitor.

Unlike almost all other waders, the green sandpiper does not build a nest on the ground. It uses old **nests** of thrushes, wood pigeons, crows or jays that lie in trees. The female usually lays four eggs, which both parents sit on for about 22 to 24 days. The male sits mainly at night.

The chicks are **nidifugous**, which means they can walk soon after hatching. But because the nest is often several metres up, they have to jump down. Thanks to their light weight and their downy plumage, they usually land unhurt on the soft forest floor. Afterwards the parents lead them to watering places, where they look for food themselves.

The green sandpiper looks for its food in shallow water and on the bank. It eats water insects and their larvae, small crustaceans, worms and sometimes small fish. It probes in the mud with its long bill. It is often looking for food at **dusk**.

The green sandpiper is a **migratory bird**. From June onwards the first birds leave their breeding areas in Scandinavia. They spend the winter in western Europe, in the Mediterranean region, in Africa and in southern Asia. On the way they also rest at small waters, ditches and sewage ponds, which is why you can watch them well in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long-legged bird that looks for food in shallow water.
A young bird that can already walk and leave the nest soon after hatching.
The lower back of a bird right above the tail.
A wet wood in which the ground is often under water.

gewusst: The green sandpiper is one of the very few waders that nest in trees.
The parent birds carry the eggshells away at once after hatching, so that enemies do not find the nest.

teile.einleitung: Buzz pollination is a special trick with which bumblebees and other bees pollinate flowers. They hold on to the flower and make their flight muscles vibrate quickly, so that the pollen is shaken out. Without this trick, tomatoes, blueberries and potatoes would be pollinated much less well.
wichtigste: In buzz pollination, bees shake the flower so that pollen falls out.
In German it is called Vibrationsbestäubung, or vibration pollination.
Some flowers, such as those of tomatoes, release the pollen only through small openings.
Bumblebees are especially good at it, but honey bees cannot do it.
The vibration comes from the flight muscles, without the wings beating.
About six to eight per cent of flowering plants depend on this method.
In greenhouses, bumblebee colonies are therefore used to pollinate tomatoes.

abschnitte.text: In **buzz pollination**, a bumblebee lands on a flower and holds on with its mouthparts. Then it tenses its **flight muscles** very quickly without beating its wings. The whole flower vibrates, and the pollen trickles out as if from a salt shaker. You often hear a loud buzzing as it does so.

In some plants the pollen sits in **anthers** that have only tiny holes at the tip. These are called poricidal anthers. The pollen comes out only if the flower is shaken hard. Examples are tomatoes, potatoes, aubergines, blueberries and cranberries.

Bumblebees are masters of buzz pollination, and many **wild bees** such as carpenter bees also manage it. The honey bee, on the other hand, cannot. The vibration is so strong that the flower experiences many times the acceleration of gravity. Wind cannot shake the pollen out as well either.

In the past, gardeners had to pollinate tomato flowers in the greenhouse laboriously by hand or with shaking devices. Since the end of the 1980s, bred **bumblebee colonies** in cardboard boxes have been used for this. That saves a lot of work and leads to nicer fruit. In Switzerland too, many tomato growers work with bumblebees.

Buzz pollination shows how closely plants and **pollinators** work together. Without bumblebees and wild bees, many plants would produce fewer fruits and seeds. Wild bees need flowering meadows and nesting places for this. Protecting bumblebees is therefore important for our food too.

begriffe.erklaerung: Passing pollen on to a flower so that fruit can form.
Fine flower dust containing the male cells of the plant.
The part of the flower in which the pollen is made.
A bee that is not kept by people, for example a bumblebee.

gewusst: When shaking, the bumblebee vibrates so fast that the note sounds higher than its normal flight buzz.
When shaking tomato flowers, bumblebees leave brown bite marks, by which gardeners can tell they have visited.
Blueberries in Swiss gardens, too, are pollinated especially well when bumblebees shake their flowers.

teile.einleitung: Vibrissae are especially long and stiff tactile hairs, like the whiskers of a cat. They are very sensitive and report even the finest touches and movements of the air to the brain. In this way animals can sense obstacles, distances and prey even in the dark.
wichtigste: Vibrissae are long, stiff tactile hairs in many mammals.
Well-known examples are the whiskers of cats, mice and seals.
A cat feels obstacles and distances in the dark with its whiskers.
Dogs also use their tactile hairs to sense their immediate surroundings.
At the root of every vibrissa lie many nerve cells.
Vibrissae are found not only on the muzzle, but also above the eyes and on the front legs.
You should never cut off vibrissae.

abschnitte.text: **Vibrissae** are thick, long hairs that are anchored deeper in the skin than normal hairs. They sit in a **follicle** that is surrounded by a small cushion of blood. Very many nerves end there. The word comes from the Latin vibrare, which means to tremble or swing.

When a vibrissa touches something or the air moves, the hair bends slightly. This movement is strengthened at the root and reported by **nerve cells** to the brain. The brain builds a picture of the surroundings from it, almost as if with the fingertips. Some animals such as mice and rats move their vibrissae back and forth actively in order to feel.

A **cat** usually has twelve whiskers on each side of the muzzle. With them it feels obstacles and distances in the dark and checks whether it fits through an opening. It also has tactile hairs above the eyes and on the back of the front paws. In the **dog**, vibrissae sit on the muzzle, chin and above the eyes and help it to sense its immediate surroundings.

**Seals** can feel the water swirls of a swimming fish with their whiskers in murky water and follow it. Walruses find mussels on the sea floor with hundreds of tactile hairs. Rats can even recognise the surface of objects with their vibrissae. Manatees also have tactile hairs spread over the whole body.

Vibrissae should never be cut, because without them the animal is unsure and finds its way around less well. If single whiskers fall out, they normally grow back. Some cats do not like it when their whiskers bump against a narrow bowl while eating. A flat, wide **food bowl** can then help.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long, stiff tactile hair in mammals.
The ability to feel touches.
A small pocket of skin in which a hair grows.
A cell that passes signals on to the brain.

gewusst: The whiskers of a cat are about as wide as its body, so they serve as a measuring tool for narrow gaps.
A blindfolded seal can follow the trail of a fish with its whiskers alone.
People have no vibrissae, and our eyebrows and eyelashes are ordinary hairs.

teile.einleitung: The kestrel is the most common falcon in Switzerland and a small, elegant bird of prey. You can easily recognise it by the way it “stands” in the air in one spot and hovers when hunting. It often lives near people and likes to nest on church towers, barns and in nest boxes.
wichtigste: The kestrel is a small falcon with a reddish brown back spotted with dark.
Typical of it is hovering flight, in which it hangs in one place in the air.
From pylons and posts it watches for mice in the grass nearby.
Besides mice, it occasionally eats small birds, insects and lizards.
Its legs and feet are yellow, and the claws are sharp and curved.
Both parents take part in looking after the young.
In Switzerland it is fairly common and is currently not regarded as badly endangered.

abschnitte.text: The kestrel is about 31 to 37 centimetres long and has a wingspan of around 70 to 80 centimetres. The male has a **grey head** and a grey tail with a black band at the end, and the back is reddish brown with dark spots. The female is browner overall and more strongly barred. Young kestrels are more plainly coloured and look more like the female. Legs and feet are yellow, and the **claws** are sharp and curved for holding prey.

The kestrel lives in open landscapes with meadows, fields and pastures, where it can hunt mice. It is found in almost all of Europe, Asia and Africa. Very often it nests in **towns and villages**, on church towers, tall buildings and bridges, which is also where its German name, Turmfalke or “tower falcon”, comes from. In Switzerland you can see it from the Central Plateau up to over 2000 metres in the Alps.

Its main prey is **field voles** and other small rodents. It hunts from a perch, such as a pylon, or in **hovering flight**: it beats its wings quickly and holds its head quite still over one spot. When it spots a mouse, it dives down and grabs it with its claws. In addition it occasionally eats small birds, insects such as grasshoppers, and lizards.

The kestrel does not build a nest of its own, but uses wall niches, rock ledges, old crows' nests or **nest boxes**. The female usually lays 4 to 6 eggs and sits on them for about a month. The male brings food during this time, and later both parents look after the young. Shortly before they fly for the first time, the young birds practise flapping their wings at the edge of the nest. At about a month old they are ready to fly.

The kestrel is fairly common in Switzerland and is currently not regarded as badly endangered. Problems are the disappearance of meadows rich in species and a lack of nesting places on modern buildings. Many people therefore put up special **nest boxes** on barns, silos and houses. Nature conservation societies and the Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach support such projects.

In the past the kestrel was regarded in **falconry** as a falcon for beginners, because it was easier to train. For hunting larger game, however, it was too small. Today, because of its hovering flight, it is one of the best-known birds of prey of all. Even children can easily watch it from the roadside on a car journey.

begriffe.erklaerung: A kind of flight in which a bird stays in one spot in the air with quick wingbeats.
A bird that grabs its prey with the claws of its feet.
A raised seat from which a bird looks out for prey.
When a young bird can fly and leaves the nest.

gewusst: Kestrels can see ultraviolet light and so can spot the urine trails of mice.
A kestrel needs about four to eight mice a day.
Some kestrels nest in the middle of big cities such as Zurich or Basel.

teile.einleitung: A bird bath is a shallow place with water in a garden or on a balcony where birds can drink and bathe. Especially in hot summers and in towns, birds often find hardly any open water. With a simple dish, any child can help the birds and watch them from close up at the same time.
wichtigste: A bird bath offers birds water to drink and bathe in.
Great tits and many other birds like to take a bird bath in summer to keep clean.
The bath should be shallow so that no bird drowns.
The water has to be changed often and the dish cleaned regularly.
A good place is one with a clear view, so that cats cannot sneak up.
Insects such as bees and animals such as hedgehogs also drink at watering places.
In winter ice-free water helps, but you must never add salt or antifreeze.

abschnitte.text: A bird bath is a container of water that people put out for wild birds. It can be a dish of clay or stone that you buy, but also an upturned **flowerpot saucer**. In the past there were puddles, streams and pools everywhere. Today many soils in towns are covered with asphalt, and rainwater flows quickly into the drains.

Birds bathe to keep their **plumage** clean and healthy. Great tits, blackbirds and sparrows hop into the water, dip their bellies in and shake their wings. Afterwards they clean every feather with the beak. Many birds spread oil from the **preen gland** as they do so, so that the feathers stay water-repellent.

The dish should be only a few centimetres deep at the edge and slope gently towards the middle. A rough bottom or a few flat stones give the birds a good grip. It is best if the bath stands raised on a base or hangs from a branch. A distance of about two metres from dense bushes protects against **cats**, which could hide there.

At a dirty bath, diseases such as **trichomonads** or salmonella can spread from bird to bird. That is why it is best to change the water daily in summer. The dish is scrubbed regularly with hot water and a brush. Washing-up liquid or cleaning products do not belong in a bird bath.

A bath does not help only birds. Bees, bumblebees and butterflies also need water and like to land on a stone that sticks out of the water. A shallow dish on the ground is also used by hedgehogs at night. In this way the garden becomes a small habitat for many animals.

At a bird bath you can watch birds very well. With an identification book or an app, you can tell great tit, blue tit, robin and chaffinch apart. Anyone who sits quietly behind a window often sees many different species in a single day. Some families note down their observations and report them in bird counts.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the feathers of a bird together.
A gland above the tail that makes oil for oiling the feathers.
Tiny germs that can spread among birds at dirty watering places.
The daily cleaning and arranging of the feathers with the beak.

gewusst: Some birds such as sparrows take not only water baths but also dust baths in dry sand.
Blackbirds sometimes bathe so thoroughly that afterwards they can hardly fly properly and first have to dry off.

teile.einleitung: A truffle pig is a specially trained domestic pig that finds hidden truffle fungi in the ground. Truffles grow underground on tree roots and are very expensive edible fungi. Pigs can smell them with their fine noses even through the soil.
wichtigste: Truffle pigs are used to find hidden truffle fungi in the ground.
Truffles grow underground in partnership with trees such as oaks and hazel bushes.
The scent of ripe truffles resembles a scent signal given off by boars, so it is mainly sows that like to search for them.
One problem is that the pigs most like to eat the truffles themselves.
Today dogs are mostly used for the search.
In Italy, truffle hunting with pigs has been banned since 1985.
Truffles also grow in Switzerland, for example the Burgundy truffle.

abschnitte.text: A truffle pig is not a breed of its own, but a **domestic pig** that has been trained to search. Pigs have an excellent **sense of smell** and by nature root around in the ground with their snouts. People have used these abilities for centuries. Searching with pigs was especially well known in France, for example in the Périgord.

**Truffles** are fungi whose fruiting bodies grow underground, mostly 5 to 30 centimetres deep. They live in partnership with tree roots, which is called **mycorrhiza**. Well-known kinds are the black Périgord truffle and the white Alba truffle from Italy. Because they are so rare and smell so strongly, they often cost several thousand francs per kilogram.

Ripe truffles give off a strong scent so that animals dig them up and so spread their spores. A substance in the scent of truffles recalls a **scent signal** from male pigs. That is why female pigs in particular are very eager in the search. They can smell truffles even through several centimetres of soil.

Pigs are big and heavy and hard to stop once they have found a truffle. Often they eat the valuable fungus straight away. They also churn up the forest floor a lot and damage the web of fungal threads. That is why today it is mostly trained **truffle dogs** that are used, which only point out the find.

In Switzerland mainly the **Burgundy truffle** grows, for example in woods in the Jura, on the Central Plateau and in western Switzerland. In some cantons you need a permit for collecting, and there are limits on amounts. In this country the search is done almost only with dogs. Some municipalities even hold truffle markets in autumn.

begriffe.erklaerung: An expensive, strongly scented fungus that grows underground.
A partnership between fungi and tree roots from which both benefit.
The ability to notice scents.
Tiny particles from which new fungi grow.

gewusst: A single large white truffle has been sold at auction for more than 100 000 euros.
Pigs have such a good sense of smell that they can keep up with sniffer dogs.
Wild boar also like to dig for truffles in the forest.

teile.einleitung: Incomplete metamorphosis is one way in which some insects develop from the egg to the adult animal. There is no pupal stage: the larva already looks similar to the finished animal and gets bigger with every moult. Grasshoppers, dragonflies, aphids and bugs develop in this way.
wichtigste: In incomplete metamorphosis there is no pupal stage.
Development goes in three stages: egg, larva and adult animal.
The larvae are often called nymphs, and they already resemble the parents.
The larvae grow by moulting several times.
Grasshoppers, dragonflies, aphids, bugs and cockroaches go through an incomplete metamorphosis.
Dragonfly larvae live in the water and have a catching mask.
In complete metamorphosis, for example in the butterfly, there is on the other hand a pupa.

abschnitte.text: Experts also call incomplete metamorphosis **hemimetaboly**. A **larva** hatches from the egg that already looks like the adult insect but does not yet have finished wings. It eats, grows and moults several times. After the last moult the insect is adult and can reproduce. There is no pupa.

Insects have a hard **outer skeleton** that does not grow with them. That is why they have to shed it when they get bigger. With every moult the wing buds on the back get a little bigger. A grasshopper larva usually moults four to six times. The shed skin is called an **exuvia**.

In **complete metamorphosis** the larva looks quite different from the adult animal, like a caterpillar and a butterfly. In between lies a pupa, in which the body is completely rebuilt. Beetles, bees, flies and butterflies develop in this way. In incomplete metamorphosis this rebuilding is missing, and the animal changes only step by step.

In the **grasshopper**, the larvae look like small grasshoppers without wings. **Dragonflies** have no pupal phase, but their larvae live for years in the water and look different from the flying dragonflies. Aphids also develop from larva to adult animal without a pupa. Bugs, cockroaches, termites and earwigs belong here as well.

The kind of metamorphosis helps researchers to sort **insects** into groups. Incomplete metamorphosis is regarded as the older form in evolutionary history. Anyone who knows how an insect develops also understands where its larvae live. This is important, for example, in protecting dragonflies, which need clean water.

begriffe.erklaerung: The young form of an animal, which can look different from the adult animal.
The larva of an insect with incomplete metamorphosis.
Shedding the old skin or casing that has become too small.
A resting stage in which a larva rebuilds itself into the adult insect.

gewusst: Dragonfly larvae can live in the water for several years, while the flying dragonfly often lives only a few weeks.
In summer aphids can have offspring without males, and they give birth to live young instead of laying eggs.
The empty larval casings of dragonflies are often found on reed stems at the bank.

teile.einleitung: The spotted hyena is the largest species of hyena and lives in Africa south of the Sahara. It is known for its giggling call and is often wrongly seen as a pure scavenger. In truth it is a tireless hunter that lives in clans in which the females are in charge.
wichtigste: The spotted hyena is the largest of the four species of hyena.
It is a mistake that spotted hyenas only eat carrion, and they hunt the greater part of their food themselves.
Their jaws are so strong that they can crush thick bones.
Because it digests many bones, its droppings are often pale.
It runs up to about 60 kilometres per hour and hunts with great stamina over long distances.
The gestation lasts about 110 days, and the young are nursed for over a year.
Lions are their most important competitors for food.

abschnitte.text: The spotted hyena has a sandy to grey-brown coat with **dark spots**. Its front legs are longer than its hind legs, so the back slopes downwards towards the rear. It grows to about 1 to 1.6 metres long and can weigh around 40 to 85 kilograms. The females are bigger and heavier than the males. With its enormously strong **jaws** it can crack even thick bones.

Spotted hyenas live in Africa south of the Sahara, mainly in **savannahs** and semi-deserts. The clans in the Ngorongoro Crater and in the Serengeti in Tanzania are very well known. But they are also found in mountain forests up to about 4000 metres. By day they often rest in burrows in the ground or in the shade.

Contrary to a widespread mistake, spotted hyenas do not eat only carrion. They hunt wildebeest, zebras and gazelles in groups and chase their prey with great **stamina** over long distances. In doing so they reach up to about 60 kilometres per hour. They use almost everything, including skin and bones, which is why their droppings are often pale from all the calcium. In quarrels over food they bite and threaten as a pack and can even drive off single lions.

Spotted hyenas live in groups called a **clan**, which can include up to 80 animals. At the top are the females, and even the highest ranking male ranks below the females. The hyenas communicate with many sounds, and their loud, **giggling** call is famous. A long drawn-out whooping call can be heard for kilometres.

After a gestation of about 110 days, the female usually gives birth to two young in a den. The young are born with their eyes open and with teeth. The **mothers** raise the young mainly alone, and the males hardly help. The young are nursed for over a year, longer than in most other predators.

The spotted hyena's most important competitor is the **lion**, which often takes prey from it and the other way round. Lions also kill hyenas if they catch them. The species is still widespread overall, but is declining outside protected areas. The reasons are persecution by people, traps and the loss of habitat.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large family group of hyenas with a fixed ranking.
The flesh of animals that are already dead.
The time in which a young animal grows in the mother's body.
An animal that eats the same food and disputes it with another.

gewusst: Hyenas look like dogs, but are more closely related to cats and mongooses.
A spotted hyena can eat about a third of its body weight in one meal.
Young spotted hyenas often fight for their rank soon after birth.

teile.einleitung: The vicuña is the smallest of the South American camels and lives high up in the Andes. It is a slender, delicate animal with light brown fur. Its wool is regarded as one of the finest and most expensive in the world.
wichtigste: The vicuña is the smallest of the South American camels.
It lives in the high Andes of Peru, Bolivia, Chile and Argentina.
It is usually found at heights of 3500 to 5000 metres.
The vicuña is the wild form of the alpaca.
Its wool is extremely fine and very valuable.
In the 1960s the vicuña was almost extinct.
Today it is the national animal of Peru and appears on the country's coat of arms.

abschnitte.text: The vicuña is about 80 to 90 centimetres high at the shoulder and weighs only 35 to 65 kilograms. That makes it smaller than the **llama**, the alpaca and the guanaco. Its coat is cinnamon brown on top and white on the belly, and on the chest it has long white hairs. It has a long, slender neck and big eyes. Like all camels it has soft **pads** on its feet.

Vicuñas live on the **puna**, a barren grassland in the high Andes. Here the air is thin, and it is sunny by day and often icy cold at night. Their blood can take up oxygen especially well, which helps them at altitude. Their dense coat protects them from the cold.

Vicuñas eat short grasses and herbs. Their lower incisors keep growing all the time, as in rodents, which is a special feature among even-toed hoofed animals. They live in **family groups** of one stallion, several females and young. Young males form groups of their own. In danger the stallion warns with a shrill whistle.

The hairs of the vicuña are only about 12 micrometres thick, much finer than human hair. The **Incas** already prized this wool, and only nobles were allowed to wear it. They rounded up the animals, sheared them and let them go again, which is called **chaccu**. This tradition is being kept up again today, because that way the vicuñas stay wild and healthy.

Because of hunting for their fur, there were only a few thousand vicuñas left in the 1960s. Strict **protection laws** and protected areas have brought the numbers back up strongly. Today several hundred thousand animals live in the Andes again. The vicuña is the national animal of Peru and decorates the country's coat of arms.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal family with long necks that includes the dromedary, Bactrian camel, llama and vicuña.
The wild species from which a domestic animal was bred.
A long mountain range on the western side of South America.
A thousandth of a millimetre.

gewusst: A scarf made of vicuña wool can cost several thousand francs.
Vicuñas use shared dung heaps that they visit again and again.
The alpacas that you see on pastures in Switzerland are descended from the vicuña.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach is the most important centre for the study of birds in Switzerland. It lies on Lake Sempach in the canton of Lucerne and studies how the birds of the country are doing. That also includes monitoring the numbers of species such as the grey heron and protecting birds.
wichtigste: The Ornithological Institute was founded in 1924 as a ringing centre.
It is a non-profit foundation based in Sempach in the canton of Lucerne.
It studies and monitors the populations of Swiss birds, for example the grey heron.
More than 130 employees and over 2000 volunteers work for it.
Since 2015 there has been a visitor centre made of clay in Sempach.
The Institute cares for sick and injured birds.
It is financed mainly by donations.

abschnitte.text: The Institute began in **1924** as a ringing centre, in order to study bird migration over the Alps. At first it was housed in the home of Alfred Schifferli in Sempach. Since **1954** it has been an independent foundation under Swiss law. Unlike in many other countries, the Ornithological Institute therefore does not belong to the state.

The Institute watches how the number of birds in Switzerland changes. For this, experts and many **volunteers** count breeding birds and winter visitors every year. In the grey heron, for example, it is followed how many breeding colonies there are and how big they are. The results go into the **breeding bird atlas** and into the Red List of threatened bird species.

In **ringing**, a bird is given a light ring with a number on its leg. If it is found again somewhere later, we know where it has travelled and how old it became. Since 1958 the Institute has run a ringing station on the Col de Bretolet in the Valais at a height of 1923 metres. There thousands of birds cross the pass in autumn.

The Institute includes a **care station** for sick, injured and orphaned birds. There, for example, birds that have flown into a pane of glass are looked after. Where possible, the animals are released again after they have recovered. Anyone who finds an injured bird can get advice from the Institute.

Since **2015** there has been a visitor centre in Sempach that is regarded as the first three-storey clay building in Switzerland. In the exhibition, children and adults experience the world of birds with games, films and mounted animals. Outside there is a garden with a pond and nesting places. Many school classes visit the centre every year.

Besides the head office there are regional offices in Sion, Contone, Chur and Yverdon-les-Bains. The Institute advises authorities, farmers and municipalities on how to protect birds. It helps, for example, to improve habitats for the skylark, lapwing and little owl. It also works internationally, for example on an action plan for migratory birds between Africa and Eurasia.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird is given a ring with a number so that it can be recognised later.
An organisation that serves a particular good cause and does not belong to the state.
The number of animals of a species that live in an area.
A list that shows which species are threatened.

gewusst: Every year the Institute gets many calls from people who have found young birds that often need no help at all.
Hundreds of thousands of birds have already been ringed on the Col de Bretolet.

teile.einleitung: The wolverine is the largest land-living member of the weasel family in the world and lives in the cold forests and tundras of the north. It looks like a small, shaggy bear and is known for its strength and stamina. Despite its German name Vielfrass, meaning glutton, it does not eat more than other animals, but it makes use of any food it finds.
wichtigste: The wolverine is the largest land-living member of the weasel family in the world.
It is clearly bigger and heavier than most other members of the weasel family.
It lives in cold northern regions such as Scandinavia, Siberia, Canada and Alaska.
Besides prey it has killed itself, it likes to eat carrion, that is, animals that are already dead.
